questions.stem: The FUNCTIONAL UNIT of the KIDNEY is the:

options.option_text: NEPHRON — each kidney has ~1 million nephrons; filter ~180 L/day, producing ~1.5 L urine; Bowman's capsule + glomerulus + tubule system

questions.explanation: NEPHRON — microscopic FUNCTIONAL + STRUCTURAL UNIT of the KIDNEY. Each kidney has ~1 MILLION (1,000,000+) nephrons. STRUCTURE: (1) RENAL CORPUSCLE — filtering unit: (a) GLOMERULUS — tuft of capillaries; (b) BOWMAN's CAPSULE — cup-like structure around glomerulus. (2) RENAL TUBULE — long winding tube: (a) PCT (Proximal Convoluted Tubule); (b) LOOP OF HENLE (descending + ascending limb, in medulla); (c) DCT (Distal Convoluted Tubule); (d) COLLECTING DUCT (shared by many nephrons; drains into renal pelvis). FUNCTIONS: (1) ULTRAFILTRATION — blood pressure pushes plasma through glomerular capillaries (with proteins + cells retained) into Bowman's capsule. GFR (Glomerular Filtration Rate) normally ~125 mL/min = 180 L/day. But we produce only ~1-2 L URINE /DAY — most water + solutes reabsorbed. (2) SELECTIVE REABSORPTION — PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtrate (glucose, amino acids, 100% normally; Na, water, bicarbonate, K). Loop of Henle establishes medullary gradient. DCT fine-tunes Na + K + H+; regulated by ALDOSTERONE. Collecting duct final water reabsorption by ADH. (3) SECRETION — H+, K+, urea, drugs, toxins into tubule. (4) EXCRETION — final urine. KIDNEYS FUNCTIONS: (1) REMOVE nitrogenous WASTES — urea (from protein metabolism in liver via Urea cycle), uric acid (purine metabolism), creatinine (muscle). (2) MAINTAIN WATER + ELECTROLYTE balance (Na, K, Cl, bicarbonate, Ca, Mg, phosphate). (3) ACID-BASE balance (blood pH 7.35-7.45; kidney excretes H+, reabsorbs HCO3-). (4) BLOOD PRESSURE regulation (RAAS — Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System; renin from JG cells). (5) RBC PRODUCTION — EPO (Erythropoietin) stimulates bone marrow → RBC. Synthetic EPO (recombinant) for anaemic renal failure patients + notoriously abused by cyclists (Lance Armstrong). (6) ACTIVATE VITAMIN D (1-α-hydroxylase). (7) GLUCONEOGENESIS (minor). KIDNEY ANATOMY: (1) Two BEAN-SHAPED organs; each ~12 cm × 6 cm × 3 cm; ~150 g each. (2) Located in RETROPERITONEUM (behind peritoneum) at T12-L3 vertebrae; right kidney slightly LOWER (liver above). (3) Regions: CORTEX (outer, contains renal corpuscles + PCT/DCT), MEDULLA (inner, renal pyramids, Loop of Henle + collecting ducts), PELVIS (funnel collecting urine into ureter). (4) Renal artery + renal vein + ureter + nerves enter/exit at HILUM. (5) URETER — 25-30 cm tube; carries urine to URINARY BLADDER. (6) BLADDER — 400-600 mL capacity. (7) URETHRA — 4 cm (women) / 20 cm (men); passes urine out; men also passes semen. (8) HORMONES affecting kidneys: ADH (water retention), Aldosterone (Na retention), ANP (natriuresis), PTH (Ca retention), calcitriol (Ca/P), catecholamines. COMPOSITION of URINE: 95% water; 2% urea; 2% salts; glucose + proteins ABSENT in healthy; pH 4.5-8; 1-2 L/day. YELLOW color from urobilin. KIDNEY DISEASES: (1) KIDNEY STONES (renal calculi) — Ca oxalate most common (75%); causes colicky severe pain; treated with hydration + ESWL (shock-wave lithotripsy) + ureteroscopy + PCNL. (2) UTI (Urinary Tract Infection) — women more prone (short urethra); E. coli most common. Burning, frequency, cloudy urine. (3) CKD (Chronic Kidney Disease) — stages 1-5 based on GFR; diabetes + hypertension leading causes worldwide + India. ~8 CR CKD patients in India. Stage 5 = ESRD (End-Stage Renal Disease); needs DIALYSIS or TRANSPLANT. (4) ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (AKI) — sudden; often reversible. (5) GLOMERULONEPHRITIS (inflammation of glomeruli — IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, post-streptococcal). (6) NEPHROTIC SYNDROME — proteinuria >3.5 g/day + low albumin + oedema + high cholesterol. (7) POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE (genetic; cysts, eventually fail). HEMODIALYSIS — 3×/week; artificial kidney via machine (Kolff 1943); 4-5 hr sessions. PERITONEAL DIALYSIS — home-based, peritoneum as filter. TRANSPLANT — best outcome; 10+ year graft survival. India: PM National Dialysis Programme (2016); Ayushman Bharat covers dialysis; 10,000+ dialysis centres.

questions.stem: The LIVER's main role in EXCRETION is:

options.option_text: Converting toxic AMMONIA (from protein breakdown) into UREA (via UREA CYCLE / Krebs-Henseleit cycle 1932); urea then excreted by kidneys

questions.explanation: LIVER's ROLE in EXCRETION: converts toxic metabolic wastes into less-toxic forms for eventual excretion by kidneys/bile/lungs. KEY CONVERSIONS: (1) UREA CYCLE (Krebs-Henseleit cycle) — in hepatocytes (liver cells); converts toxic AMMONIA (NH₃, from deamination of proteins) into UREA (NH₂)₂CO — less toxic, water-soluble, easy to excrete by kidneys. ~30 g/day urea produced. (2) BILIRUBIN metabolism — from broken-down RBCs; liver conjugates with glucuronic acid → water-soluble; excreted in bile → intestine → stool (gives brown colour; urobilin small amount in urine = yellow). Excess unconjugated = JAUNDICE (hemolysis, neonatal, Gilbert syndrome). Excess conjugated = biliary obstruction (stones, cancer, hepatitis). (3) CHOLESTEROL — excreted in bile; removed by stool. (4) DRUG METABOLISM — CYP450 enzymes + conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) — 'first-pass metabolism'; drugs often inactivated or activated (prodrugs); 70-90% of drug metabolism in liver. (5) HORMONES — inactivated here. LIVER also produces UREA + many other biomolecules. LIVER ANATOMY: (1) LARGEST INTERNAL organ (1.5 kg in adult; 2nd to skin as largest organ); 4 lobes; right 2/3 + left 1/3. In RIGHT UPPER quadrant of abdomen; mostly protected by ribs. DUAL BLOOD SUPPLY — hepatic artery (25%, oxygen-rich) + portal vein (75%, nutrient-rich from intestines). Hepatic veins → IVC → heart. (2) STRUCTURAL UNIT: LOBULE — hexagonal; portal triad (hepatic artery + portal vein + bile duct) at corners; central vein at center; hepatocytes arranged radially. (3) BILE — 500-1000 mL/day; stored + concentrated in GALL BLADDER (85 mL capacity, under liver); released into DUODENUM via bile duct during digestion (triggered by CCK when fats arrive). Emulsifies fats for lipase action. Contains bile salts + cholesterol + bilirubin + water. (4) >500 FUNCTIONS — 'chemical factory of the body'. LIVER FUNCTIONS: (1) METABOLISM — carbohydrate (glucose ↔ glycogen; gluconeogenesis); fat (lipoprotein synthesis — LDL, HDL, VLDL; cholesterol; ketogenesis during fasting); protein (albumin, clotting factors — II, VII, IX, X, fibrinogen; transport proteins — transferrin, ceruloplasmin, haptoglobin). (2) DETOXIFICATION — ammonia → urea; drug + alcohol + toxin metabolism. (3) BILE PRODUCTION. (4) STORAGE — glycogen (~100 g), iron, vit A, D, E, K, B12, Cu. (5) IMMUNE — Kupffer cells (fixed macrophages). (6) BLOOD production (in fetus). LIVER DISEASES: (1) HEPATITIS — inflammation; viral (A, B, C, D, E — A + E fecal-oral, B + C + D blood-sexual); vaccines available for A + B (B since 1982); C curable since 2013 with DAAs (direct-acting antivirals; sofosbuvir; near 95%+ cure); D only with B; E esp dangerous in pregnancy. (2) CIRRHOSIS — end-stage fibrosis; alcohol + hep B/C + NAFLD leading causes. (3) NAFLD (Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease) — OBESITY/diabetes driven; 20-40% of Indian adults. Can progress to NASH + cirrhosis + HCC. (4) HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA (HCC) — liver cancer, esp with cirrhosis. (5) WILSON's DISEASE (genetic copper overload); HEMOCHROMATOSIS (iron); GILBERT syndrome (mild hyperbilirubinemia). LIVER TRANSPLANT — 2nd most common solid organ transplant after kidney; both CDVs + LDLT (living donor liver transplant — partial lobe). India: 3,000+ transplants/yr; ILBS Delhi, Apollo, Medanta top centres. NATIONAL ORGAN + TISSUE TRANSPLANT ORG (NOTTO). LUNGS also excrete — CO₂ + water vapour. SKIN — sweat (water + salts + urea). INTESTINE — undigested fibre + bile acids. EXCRETORY PRODUCTS: UREA (terrestrial mammals = ureotelic), URIC ACID (birds + reptiles = uricotelic, saves water), AMMONIA (fish + amphibians = ammonotelic, requires lots of water).

questions.stem: NORMAL composition of URINE — what percentage is water?

options.option_text: ~95% water + 2% urea + 2% salts + 1% other (creatinine, uric acid, hormones, pigments); yellow color from UROBILIN; daily volume 1-2 L

questions.explanation: URINE COMPOSITION (healthy adult): (1) WATER — ~95%. (2) UREA — 2% (~25-30 g/day; protein metabolism end-product). (3) SODIUM CHLORIDE + other SALTS — 2% (NaCl, KCl, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, phosphates, sulfates, bicarbonate). (4) CREATININE — 0.1% (from muscle creatine phosphate breakdown; excretion relatively constant; used as kidney function marker — serum creatinine rises in renal failure). (5) URIC ACID — 0.04% (from purine breakdown). (6) AMMONIA, hormones (urobilinogen, cortisol), small amounts. (7) TRACE substances — drugs, toxins, dyes (asparagus makes urine smell; beetroot turns pink). VOLUME: 1-2 L/DAY (adults); varies with fluid intake, sweat, ambient temp. Night urine lower (anti-diuretic hormone rise during sleep). SPECIFIC GRAVITY: 1.005-1.030 (concentrated urine denser). pH: 4.5-8 (avg 6, slightly acidic); varies with diet (meat lowers pH, vegetables raise). CAN check pH with urine test strips. COLOR: pale yellow → straw → amber; UROBILIN (bilirubin breakdown) + urochrome give yellow; darker urine = more concentrated (dehydration). ABNORMAL colors: (a) RED — blood (haematuria — bladder/kidney infection/stones/cancer; also beetroot, rhubarb, food colouring); (b) ORANGE — rifampin (TB drug), carrot excess; (c) GREEN/BLUE — methylene blue, Pseudomonas infection, propofol anaesthesia, familial benign blue urine; (d) BROWN / COLA — severe dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, porphyria, hepatic disorders (bilirubinuria); (e) FOAMY — proteinuria (kidney disease). DIAGNOSTIC TESTS: (1) URINE ROUTINE + MICROSCOPY (U R/M) — basic screening: pH + SG + protein + glucose + ketones + blood + bilirubin + leukocytes + nitrites + RBCs/WBCs/casts/crystals microscopically. (2) URINE CULTURE — bacterial identification + antibiogram. (3) 24-HOUR URINE COLLECTION — protein, creatinine clearance (GFR estimate), electrolytes. (4) URINE MICROALBUMIN — early diabetic kidney disease. (5) URINE hCG — pregnancy test (hCG is Human Chorionic Gonadotropin from trophoblast; urine tests detect 25 mIU/mL). ABNORMAL URINE findings: (a) PROTEIN — glomerular damage. (b) GLUCOSE — uncontrolled diabetes. (c) KETONES — starvation, DKA. (d) BLOOD — UTIs, stones, cancer. (e) BILIRUBIN — liver disease. (f) NITRITES + LEUKOCYTES — UTI. (g) CRYSTALS — stones risk. (h) CASTS (RBC, WBC, granular, hyaline) — nephritis. (i) SEDIMENT — various. UTI (Urinary Tract Infection) — most common bacterial infection globally; 50% of women experience at least once in lifetime. E. coli most common (80%); also Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Klebsiella. Ascending infection from urethra. SYMPTOMS: burning + frequency + urgency + cloudy/smelly urine + suprapubic pain. Treat with antibiotics (nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin). Complicated UTI → PYELONEPHRITIS (kidney infection) with fever + flank pain + vomiting. SEPSIS risk. URINARY INCONTINENCE — involuntary urine loss; common elderly + post-pregnancy + neurological. Types: stress (cough-sneeze), urge (detrusor overactivity), overflow (obstruction), functional. Treatment: Kegel exercises, meds, surgery (sling), devices. URINARY STONES (calculi) — 12% of men + 6% of women develop; 75% calcium oxalate; also Ca phosphate, uric acid, struvite, cystine. Extreme pain ('renal colic' — 'worse than childbirth' per some). Treatment: hydration + alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) for small stones; ESWL (Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy), ureteroscopy with LASER, PCNL for large.

questions.stem: The HORMONE that regulates WATER REABSORPTION in kidney tubules is:

options.option_text: ADH (Anti-Diuretic Hormone, Vasopressin) — made in HYPOTHALAMUS, stored in POSTERIOR PITUITARY; acts on V2 receptors of collecting ducts to insert aquaporins

questions.explanation: ADH (ANTI-DIURETIC HORMONE) / VASOPRESSIN / AVP — 9-amino acid peptide hormone that regulates WATER REABSORPTION in kidneys. Made in HYPOTHALAMUS (supraoptic + paraventricular nuclei), stored + released from POSTERIOR PITUITARY GLAND. MECHANISM: (1) ADH binds V2 RECEPTORS on collecting duct principal cells. (2) G-protein signaling → cAMP → inserts AQUAPORIN-2 (AQP2) water channels into apical membrane. (3) Water passively reabsorbed (down osmotic gradient established by Loop of Henle). (4) MORE ADH = MORE water reabsorbed = CONCENTRATED urine + less volume. Less ADH = dilute urine + more volume. TRIGGERS for ADH release: (1) PLASMA OSMOLALITY — > 285 mOsm/kg (dehydration) → osmoreceptors in hypothalamus → ADH release; results in water conservation. Main trigger. (2) BLOOD VOLUME / PRESSURE — hypovolemia (haemorrhage) → baroreceptors in carotid sinus + aortic arch → ADH release; less sensitive. (3) Stress, nicotine, morphine, nausea stimulate ADH. (4) Ethanol SUPPRESSES ADH → WATER DIURESIS + DEHYDRATION (hence drinking alcohol = pee more = hangover next day partly dehydration). CLINICAL DISORDERS: (1) DIABETES INSIPIDUS (DI) — ADH deficit or resistance → excessive DILUTE urine (>3 L/day, up to 20 L), severe thirst (polydipsia). 2 types: (a) CENTRAL DI (Pituitary DI) — ADH not produced; causes: head trauma, pituitary tumor, surgery, infection. Treat with DDAVP (desmopressin, synthetic ADH analog, nasal spray or tablet). (b) NEPHROGENIC DI — kidneys don't respond to ADH; causes: lithium (bipolar), hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, genetic. Treat underlying cause + thiazide diuretics paradoxically. Differ from Diabetes Mellitus (sugar problem). Testing: water deprivation test + DDAVP response. (2) SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH) — EXCESS ADH; retains too much water → dilutional HYPONATREMIA (low Na); confusion, seizures, coma if severe. Causes: small-cell lung cancer (ectopic secretion), CNS infections, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, NSAIDs). Treatment: fluid restriction + vaptans (tolvaptan V2 antagonist) + demeclocycline. OTHER HORMONES affecting KIDNEY: (1) ALDOSTERONE — from adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa); RAAS pathway — stimulated by low BP, high K, low Na. Acts on DCT/collecting duct to RETAIN Na + WATER + excrete K + H. Primary aldosteronism = Conn's syndrome (adenoma, hypertension, low K). Hypoaldosteronism = Addison's disease. (2) ANP (Atrial Natriuretic Peptide) — from atria of heart when stretched (high BP); promotes Na + water EXCRETION; OPPOSITE of aldosterone; physiological diuretic. Also BNP (brain/B-type NP). BNP test used for diagnosing heart failure (elevated in CHF). (3) ANGIOTENSIN II — potent vasoconstrictor; stimulates aldosterone; made from angiotensin I by ACE (Angiotensin Converting Enzyme, in lungs). ACE-inhibitors (ramipril, enalapril, lisinopril) treat hypertension + heart failure by blocking this. ARBs (losartan, telmisartan) block AT1 receptors. (4) PARATHYROID HORMONE — raises Ca reabsorption, phosphate excretion. (5) CALCITRIOL — vitamin D active form; Ca absorption. (6) ERYTHROPOIETIN (EPO) — stimulates RBC production; synthetic EPO (Epoetin alpha) for anaemia in CKD; famous for doping in Tour de France (Lance Armstrong). (7) THYROID hormones, cortisol affect kidneys indirectly. RAAS CASCADE: Low BP/Na → JG cells secrete RENIN → converts angiotensinogen (liver) to Angiotensin I → ACE (lungs) → Angiotensin II (vasoconstrictor + aldosterone stimulant + ADH stimulant) → increases BP + fluid. Central to HYPERTENSION + HEART FAILURE management.
questions.subject: Biology

options.option_text: KIDNEY FAILURE — artificial filtration of waste + excess water from blood; HEMODIALYSIS (machine, 3x/week) or PERITONEAL DIALYSIS (home-based)

questions.explanation: DIALYSIS — artificial process of filtering waste products + excess water from the blood when KIDNEYS FAIL. Invented 1943 by Dutch physician WILLEM KOLFF (in Nazi-occupied Netherlands; first practical dialysis machine) — 'Father of Dialysis'. 2 MAIN TYPES: (1) HEMODIALYSIS (HD) — MACHINE-based. Blood drawn from patient via vascular access (AV fistula — arteriovenous surgical connection in forearm; or catheter); pumped through DIALYZER (artificial kidney) with semi-permeable membrane; dialysate (electrolyte solution) on other side; wastes + excess water move across by DIFFUSION + ULTRAFILTRATION; cleaned blood returned. Typical session: 4 HOURS × 3 TIMES/WEEK at dialysis centre. Needs heparin (blood thinner) to prevent clotting. India: govt-subsidised; Ayushman Bharat covers; 10,000+ centres; PMNDP (PM National Dialysis Programme, 2016) for poor patients. (2) PERITONEAL DIALYSIS (PD) — uses patient's own PERITONEUM (abdominal lining) as filter. (a) CAPD (Continuous Ambulatory PD) — dialysate fluid (1-3 L) via catheter into peritoneal cavity 4-5 times/day; each exchange 20-30 min; patients do themselves at home. (b) APD (Automated PD) — cycler machine does exchanges at night while sleeping. Advantages: home-based, more flexible, gentler on heart. Disadvantages: peritonitis risk (infection), less effective removal, scar development. INDICATIONS for dialysis (ESRD patients): (1) GFR <15 mL/min (Stage 5 CKD). (2) Fluid overload unresponsive. (3) Severe electrolyte disturbance (K >6.5, severe acidosis). (4) Uremic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy, severe nausea/vomiting). (5) Some drug + poisoning treatments. (6) Acute kidney injury temporarily. COMPLICATIONS of dialysis: hypotension, cramps, access infections, bleeding, amyloidosis (long-term), sleep disturbance, malnutrition, cardiovascular disease (leading cause of death in dialysis patients). AVG survival 5-10 years on dialysis; transplant better. TRANSPLANT ALTERNATIVE — BETTER long-term outcome: (1) Deceased donor transplant (cadaveric) — organs from brain-dead donors. (2) Living-related donor (spouse, sibling, parent) — 10+ year graft survival. India: ~8,000-10,000 kidney transplants/year. 1st in India: 1971 Chennai. NEED: ~2 LAKH+ kidney transplants/year but only ~10,000 done due to donor shortage. ORGAN DONATION rates in India remain LOW (~1 per million pop vs Spain 46, USA 27; improving). TRANSPLANT LAWS: Transplantation of Human Organs + Tissues Act 1994; NOTTO (National Organ + Tissue Transplant Organisation, Delhi 2014); ROTTO (regional) + SOTTO (state). COMMERCIAL organ trade ILLEGAL globally except Iran (debated). KIDNEY FAILURE CAUSES globally: (1) DIABETES (#1 — 40%); (2) HYPERTENSION (~25%); (3) GLOMERULONEPHRITIS; (4) POLYCYSTIC KIDNEY DISEASE (genetic); (5) OBSTRUCTIVE uropathy; (6) Chronic pyelonephritis. INDIA: ~8 CRORE CKD patients. Many never diagnosed. ANEMIA + CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE + BONE-MINERAL disorder complications. SCREENING + PREVENTION: (a) annual BP + blood sugar + urine microalbumin after 40; (b) control diabetes + hypertension; (c) avoid NSAIDs chronic use; (d) hydration. OTHER EXCRETORY aids: (1) ACTIVATED CHARCOAL (for drug overdoses); (2) IONIC RESINS (kayexalate for K; renagel for P); (3) Alkalinisation (sodium bicarbonate); (4) hemoperfusion (for some poisonings). ARTIFICIAL KIDNEY — goal of bio-engineering (implantable); clinical trials ongoing. XENOTRANSPLANT — pig kidneys genetically modified — 1st human kidney xenotransplant 2024 (Massachusetts General — patient lived 2 months).

questions.stem: SWEAT, produced by sweat glands, serves dual purpose. Besides cooling the body, sweat also:

options.option_text: EXCRETES small quantities of WASTE — urea, lactate, salts (NaCl), ammonia, some drugs; minor excretory role + body's cooling mechanism via evaporation

questions.explanation: SWEAT (perspiration) — salty liquid secreted by SWEAT GLANDS in the SKIN (dermis). Two types of sweat glands: (1) ECCRINE glands — 2-4 MILLION distributed all over body (most abundant on palms, soles, forehead); open directly to skin; produce WATERY sweat; primary for thermoregulation. Active from infancy. (2) APOCRINE glands — in armpits + groin + areola (around nipples); open into hair follicles; produce THICKER + fattier sweat; active from puberty; bacterial breakdown causes BODY ODOUR. SWEAT COMPOSITION: 99% WATER + 1% SOLUTES — NaCl (main), K, Ca, urea, lactate, ammonia, trace metals. Contains ~0.1% of body's salt. Can lose 1-2 L/hour in hot conditions; marathon runners 3 L/hr; can lose 10-15 L/day in extreme heat + exercise. FUNCTIONS: (1) THERMOREGULATION — MAJOR function; evaporation cools skin (each gram of sweat evaporating absorbs ~540 cal latent heat). Core body temp normally 36.5-37.5°C. (2) EXCRETION — minor: 5% of body's urea; 2% of NaCl; some drugs (penicillin, lithium). Not primary excretion route. (3) pH — slightly acidic (~4-7); protects against bacteria. (4) Apocrine sweat has pheromonal function (debated humans; clear in animals). CONTROL: (a) HYPOTHALAMUS (preoptic area) — body's thermostat. (b) SYMPATHETIC nerves (cholinergic, unusually — ACh for eccrine; adrenergic for apocrine). (c) TRIGGERS — heat (thermal sweating), exercise, fever (eccrine; body cools); STRESS / emotions (emotional sweating — palms/soles/armpits; apocrine). HEAT ILLNESSES: (1) HEAT CRAMPS — salt depletion. (2) HEAT EXHAUSTION — fatigue, dizziness, nausea; sweating+weak. (3) HEAT STROKE — medical emergency; core temp >40°C, NO sweating (thermoregulation failed); confusion; mortality high. Treat with rapid cooling + hydration. (4) DEHYDRATION — 1% body weight loss impairs performance; 3% noticeable; 10% dangerous. INDIA's HEAT WAVES becoming more frequent + lethal — 2022, 2023, 2024 all records; 100s of deaths each year; climate change projections worsening. Heat action plans required (NDMA). DRINK WATER + ORS + stay indoors midday in summer. SKIN ABNORMALITIES: (1) HYPERHIDROSIS — excessive sweating; focal (palms, soles, armpits) or generalised; treat with antiperspirants (aluminium chloride), iontophoresis, botox injections, sympathectomy. (2) ANHIDROSIS — decreased/absent sweating; can cause heat intolerance; congenital or due to drugs/neurological. (3) BROMHIDROSIS — foul-smelling sweat (usually apocrine + bacteria). SKIN — LARGEST organ of body (2 sq m in adult; 4-5 kg; 15% body weight). 3 LAYERS: (1) EPIDERMIS (outer) — 5 strata; keratinocytes + melanocytes (skin color) + Langerhans cells (immune) + Merkel cells (touch). Replaced every 28-30 days. No blood vessels. (2) DERMIS — blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, sebaceous glands (oil), hair follicles, collagen + elastin fibres; touch + pain + pressure + temperature receptors. (3) HYPODERMIS (subcutaneous) — fat for insulation + energy. FUNCTIONS of SKIN: (1) BARRIER (physical, chemical, biological). (2) THERMOREGULATION — sweat + vasodilation/constriction. (3) SENSATION. (4) VIT D synthesis (UV + 7-dehydrocholesterol → cholecalciferol). (5) EXCRETION — minor (sweat, sebum). (6) IMMUNE (Langerhans cells + skin-associated lymphoid tissue SALT). (7) BLOOD reservoir. (8) Absorption (small; some drugs as patches). SEBUM from SEBACEOUS glands — oily; protects skin + hair; excessive = acne when pores blocked.

questions.stem: BIRDS excrete nitrogenous waste mainly as:

options.option_text: URIC ACID — semi-solid white paste; saves WATER; suitable for flight (low weight) + shelled eggs (non-toxic to embryo)

questions.explanation: NITROGENOUS WASTE EXCRETION modes in ANIMALS: (1) AMMONOTELIC — excrete AMMONIA (NH₃) directly. Simple, 1 step from amino acid deamination; BUT very toxic (requires dilution ~400 mL H₂O per 1 g N). Feasible only for AQUATIC animals — FISH (freshwater), AMPHIBIANS' tadpoles, many invertebrates (worms, crustaceans, molluscs). Ammonia diffuses out through gills + skin to water. Cheap metabolically. (2) UREOTELIC — excrete UREA. Mammals, adult amphibians, sharks, terrestrial turtles. Urea synthesised in LIVER (UREA CYCLE, Krebs-Henseleit 1932) from ammonia + CO₂ + ATP — energy cost BUT much less toxic + need ~50 mL water/g N. Allows land life where water conservation matters. Humans produce ~25-30 g urea/day. EQUATION: 2 NH₃ + CO₂ → (NH₂)₂CO + H₂O; in liver: CPS-I + ornithine + citrulline + argininosuccinate + arginine + urea = 5-step cycle. (3) URICOTELIC — excrete URIC ACID. Birds, reptiles, insects, some land snails, terrestrial arthropods. Uric acid is SEMI-SOLID (crystalline) paste + virtually NON-TOXIC + requires minimum water (<10 mL/g N). Enables: (a) FLIGHT in birds (reduced water weight); (b) EGG viability (embryo's waste in closed shell can accumulate as harmless uric acid crystals); (c) DESERT survival in reptiles. Synthesised from purines via xanthine oxidase. High energy cost but high water conservation. BIRD DROPPINGS: WHITE part = uric acid crystals (urine); dark GREEN-BROWN = faeces. Both excreted together from CLOACA (single vent — urogenital + digestive combined). Reptiles similar. HUMANS also produce uric acid from purine metabolism (meat + organ meats + alcohol + fructose → high uric acid); normal serum 3-7 mg/dL; excess = GOUT (urate crystals deposit in joints — big toe classic, 'podagra'; red, swollen, painful joint; treatment: NSAIDs acute + allopurinol/febuxostat chronic). Kidney stones = ~10% uric acid. (4) GUANOTELIC — Excretion of GUANINE. Rare; spiders, scorpions (arachnids), penguins (partial). OTHER EXCRETORY ORGANS in animals: (1) CONTRACTILE VACUOLE — amoeba, paramecium, freshwater protozoans; expels excess water. (2) FLAME CELLS / PROTONEPHRIDIA — flatworms; filtration via beating flagella. (3) METANEPHRIDIA — segmented worms (earthworms — 2 per segment); open to coelom + exterior. (4) GREEN GLANDS / ANTENNAL GLANDS — crustaceans (prawns, crabs). (5) MALPIGHIAN TUBULES — insects; blind-ending tubules in hemocoel; filter + excrete URIC ACID via gut. Hundreds in locusts. Highly water-efficient — key to insects' land success. (6) COXAL GLANDS — arachnids. (7) NEPHRIDIA — polychaete worms. (8) HENLE's LOOP in kidney — hallmark of mammals + some birds; allows concentrated urine. (9) SALT GLANDS — marine birds (albatrosses, penguins) + reptiles (sea turtles, iguanas) + sharks; excrete hypertonic saline ('crying' turtles). WATER + SALT BALANCE: (a) FRESHWATER fish — tend to GAIN water osmotically + LOSE salts; drink little; produce dilute urine; active salt uptake via gills. (b) MARINE fish — tend to LOSE water + gain salts; drink seawater; produce concentrated urine; actively secrete NaCl via gills. Sharks use urea as osmolyte to be isoosmotic with seawater. (c) Mammals — kidney concentrates urine up to 4× plasma (humans); desert animals even higher (kangaroo rat 17×, Australia's hopping mouse 25×). (d) Marine mammals (whales, seals) — concentrated urine; drink little seawater. HIBERNATION / aestivation — reduced metabolism + waste production. URIC ACID is the END PRODUCT in humans too (for PURINES specifically) — not primary like birds.

questions.stem: The GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately:

options.option_text: 125 mL/min (~180 L/day); decreases with age; eGFR < 60 indicates Chronic Kidney Disease; < 15 = end-stage needing dialysis/transplant

questions.explanation: GFR (GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE) — key indicator of KIDNEY FUNCTION; rate at which kidneys FILTER blood. Normal healthy adult: ~125 mL/MIN (180 L/DAY). Total blood volume ~5 L, so blood is filtered ~35 times per day! But we produce only 1-2 L urine — 99% of filtrate reabsorbed. DETERMINED by: (1) NET FILTRATION PRESSURE — (a) glomerular capillary BP (+60 mmHg; driving force); (b) Bowman's capsule pressure (-15 mmHg opposing); (c) colloid osmotic pressure of plasma proteins (-25 mmHg opposing). Net = ~+10-15 mmHg outward pressure. (2) Kf (filtration coefficient) — surface area + permeability of glomerular capillaries. AUTOREGULATION: kidneys maintain GFR over BP range 80-180 mmHg via: (a) Myogenic response; (b) Tubulo-glomerular feedback (macula densa). MEASUREMENT: (1) INULIN CLEARANCE — gold standard; inulin is freely filtered + neither reabsorbed nor secreted. IV infusion + urine/plasma sampling. Precise but cumbersome. (2) CREATININE CLEARANCE — more practical; creatinine endogenous. 24-hour urine collection. (3) eGFR (estimated GFR) — calculated from SERUM CREATININE + age + sex + race using formulas. (a) MDRD equation; (b) CKD-EPI (better, now standard); (c) Cockcroft-Gault. Serum creatinine alone unreliable (varies with muscle mass — elderly + amputees have low creatinine with normal kidney function). (4) CYSTATIN C — newer biomarker; better than creatinine in some cases. CKD STAGES (per KDIGO 2012 guidelines): (a) STAGE 1: GFR ≥90 WITH kidney damage marker (protein, cyst, structural abnormality). (b) STAGE 2: 60-89 + damage. (c) STAGE 3a: 45-59. (d) STAGE 3b: 30-44. (e) STAGE 4: 15-29. (f) STAGE 5 / ESRD: <15 — require DIALYSIS or TRANSPLANT. GFR DECLINES with age — ~8 mL/min per decade after 40; by 80 years, GFR ~70. GENDER + RACE adjustments. CKD RISK factors: DIABETES (40% of CKD worldwide + India), HYPERTENSION (25%), family history, age 60+, OBESITY, smoking, analgesic overuse (NSAIDs), recurrent UTIs, obstructive uropathy. SYMPTOMS (often asymptomatic until Stage 3-4): fatigue, oedema (feet + ankles + face), itching (urea in skin), nausea, loss of appetite, muscle cramps, metallic taste, frequent urination (night — NOCTURIA), foaming urine (proteinuria). DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP: (1) Serum creatinine + eGFR + BUN (blood urea nitrogen). (2) Urinalysis — protein, casts, blood. (3) Urine ACR (albumin-creatinine ratio) — >30 mg/g = albuminuria. (4) KIDNEY USG — size, cysts, obstruction. (5) Biopsy in select cases. CKD progression risk factors: (a) Stage higher; (b) Proteinuria higher; (c) HTN uncontrolled; (d) Diabetes uncontrolled; (e) Smoking; (f) High cholesterol. MANAGEMENT: (1) TREAT UNDERLYING cause — diabetes (HbA1c <7%), BP (<130/80 mmHg), lipids. (2) ACE-inhibitor / ARB — reduces proteinuria + slows progression. (3) SGLT2 INHIBITORS (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) — NEW class; renoprotective even in non-diabetics (DAPA-CKD trial 2020; EMPA-KIDNEY 2022). GAME-CHANGERS for CKD. (4) Dietary — low protein (0.8 g/kg/day), low salt, low phosphate. (5) Treat complications: anaemia (EPO, iron), bone disease (Ca, Vit D analogues, phosphate binders), acidosis (bicarbonate). (6) Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides). INDIA: 8 CRORE CKD patients estimated. PMNDP (Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme 2016) free/subsidised dialysis. Kidney transplantation remains gold-standard treatment.

questions.stem: BILIRUBIN, the yellow pigment that causes JAUNDICE, comes from:

options.option_text: BREAKDOWN of OLD RED BLOOD CELLS (haemoglobin — heme → biliverdin → bilirubin); processed in LIVER, excreted in bile; elevated → YELLOW skin/eyes = JAUNDICE

questions.explanation: BILIRUBIN — yellow-orange PIGMENT from the breakdown of HAEMOGLOBIN in old/damaged RED BLOOD CELLS (RBCs lifespan ~120 days). PATHWAY: RBCs broken down in SPLEEN (reticuloendothelial system — macrophages, Kupffer cells in liver, bone marrow) → HAEMOGLOBIN split into: (a) HEME — iron removed (recycled to transferrin); porphyrin ring → BILIVERDIN → BILIRUBIN via biliverdin reductase. (b) GLOBIN (protein) — amino acids recycled. BILIRUBIN journey: (1) UNCONJUGATED BILIRUBIN (INSOLUBLE in water; lipid-soluble; toxic to brain especially infants) — bound to ALBUMIN in blood; carried to LIVER. (2) In LIVER — hepatocytes take up bilirubin; CONJUGATE it with GLUCURONIC ACID (via UGT1A1 enzyme) → CONJUGATED BILIRUBIN (WATER-SOLUBLE, non-toxic). (3) Conjugated bilirubin excreted in BILE → GALL BLADDER → DUODENUM. (4) In intestine — gut bacteria convert to UROBILINOGEN → partly reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation, some to urine as UROBILIN — gives yellow color) + partly oxidised to STERCOBILIN (gives stool BROWN color). ~300 mg bilirubin produced daily. JAUNDICE (icterus) — yellow discoloration of SKIN + SCLERA (whites of eyes) + mucous membranes due to serum bilirubin >2 mg/dL (normal <1 mg/dL). CLINICALLY visible when bilirubin ~2.5-3 mg/dL. TYPES of JAUNDICE (based on cause): (1) PRE-HEPATIC / HEMOLYTIC — EXCESS RBC breakdown overwhelming liver. Causes: HEMOLYTIC anaemia (SICKLE CELL, G6PD deficiency, thalassemia, autoimmune hemolysis), malaria, transfusion reaction, hereditary spherocytosis. LAB: ↑ UNCONJUGATED bilirubin; ↑ reticulocytes; ↓ haptoglobin; normal liver enzymes. (2) HEPATIC / HEPATOCELLULAR — liver CAN'T CONJUGATE or SECRETE. Causes: VIRAL HEPATITIS (A + B + C + E), ALCOHOLIC hepatitis, CIRRHOSIS, drug-induced (paracetamol overdose, isoniazid, rifampin), Gilbert + Crigler-Najjar + Dubin-Johnson syndromes, NAFLD/NASH. LAB: BOTH conjugated + unconjugated ↑; ↑ ALT + AST (hepatocyte enzymes); ↑ ALP + GGT moderately. (3) POST-HEPATIC / OBSTRUCTIVE — bile flow BLOCKED. Causes: GALLSTONES in bile duct, PANCREATIC cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, PSC (primary sclerosing cholangitis), parasites. LAB: ↑ CONJUGATED bilirubin (appears in urine = DARK urine; PALE stools because bilirubin doesn't reach intestine); ↑ ALP + GGT markedly. Imaging: USG abdomen (gall stones), MRCP + ERCP for biliary tree. (4) NEONATAL JAUNDICE — 60% of newborns; physiological (liver UGT1A1 immature) or pathological (Rh / ABO incompatibility hemolysis); severe cases → KERNICTERUS (brain damage, deafness, cerebral palsy). Treatment: phototherapy (blue light converts bilirubin to water-soluble isomers); exchange transfusion in severe. GILBERT SYNDROME — benign hereditary UGT1A1 reduced activity (~10% population); mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; jaundice with fasting/stress; harmless. CRIGLER-NAJJAR — complete UGT1A1 absence; severe; type I fatal without transplant. RECENT INDIAN FOCUS: (1) HEPATITIS B + C high burden in NE + Punjab. (2) NAFLD epidemic — 20-40% adults. (3) HEP A outbreaks via contaminated water. (4) JAUNDICE home remedies — avoid; consult doctor.

questions.stem: The LARGEST solid organ of the HUMAN body (also largest gland) is:

options.option_text: LIVER — ~1.5 kg adult; right upper abdomen; performs 500+ functions (metabolism, detox, bile, protein synthesis); can REGENERATE remarkably

questions.explanation: HUMAN BODY's ORGAN SIZES: (1) LARGEST SOLID ORGAN + LARGEST GLAND = LIVER (~1.5 kg adult; 4 lobes; right upper abdomen). 500+ functions. Unique REGENERATION ability — up to 2/3 can be removed + liver can regrow to full size in weeks (basis of LIVING DONOR LIVER TRANSPLANT — donor gives a portion, recipient gets it; both regenerate). PROMETHEUS myth anticipated this — eagle ate his liver daily which regrew. (2) LARGEST ORGAN OVERALL (including skin, which is sometimes counted) = SKIN — 2 sq m area, 4-5 kg weight, 15% body weight. (3) LARGEST INTERNAL ORGAN — Liver (or some say small intestine by length 6m). (4) LARGEST ENDOCRINE gland — PANCREAS (exocrine + endocrine both; 70-80 g; lobes in upper abdomen). (5) LARGEST PURE EXOCRINE gland — LIVER (as exocrine — makes bile). But bile is exocrine secretion. (6) LARGEST ENDOCRINE-only gland — THYROID (~20 g). (7) Largest LYMPHOID organ — SPLEEN. (8) LONGEST nerve — SCIATIC nerve (45 cm from lower back to foot). (9) LONGEST bone — FEMUR (thigh bone; ~45 cm in adult; 1/4 of body height). (10) SMALLEST bone — STAPES (middle ear; 2.8 mm; stirrup-shaped). (11) LARGEST muscle — GLUTEUS MAXIMUS (buttock). (12) SMALLEST muscle — STAPEDIUS (in middle ear; dampens stapes vibration). (13) STRONGEST muscle (by mass) — MASSETER (jaw; can bite 70-80 kg force). (14) HARDEST substance — TOOTH ENAMEL (calcium phosphate hydroxyapatite; harder than bone). (15) LARGEST blood vessel — AORTA (descending aorta 2.5-3 cm diameter). (16) TOTAL BLOOD volume — 5 L adult (8% of body weight). (17) LONGEST CELL — MOTOR NEURON (up to 1 m, from spinal cord to toe; axon). (18) LONGEST 'ORGAN' — intestines; small intestine 6 m + large intestine 1.5 m = 7.5 m. (19) Red blood cells — ~25 TRILLION in body; life 120 days; 2 million made per second. (20) Brain — 1.4 kg; 86 BILLION neurons + 85B glial cells; 20% of body's energy use. (21) Heart — 300 g; beats ~3 billion times in lifetime; pumps 7,000 L blood/day. (22) Bones — 206 in adult (270+ in newborn, many fuse). 5 layers of skin. 650+ skeletal muscles + ~900 counting smooth + cardiac. 100,000+ km blood vessels (would wrap Earth 2.5× if laid end to end). HUMAN BODY IS 60% WATER. CO₂ exhaled daily ~1 kg. BREATHS per day ~20,000. 100,000 heart beats per day. RBC production ~2 million/sec. DIGESTION 24-72 hr for food to transit. POOP weight ~100-250 g per day (varies). URINE 1-2 L. COOLANTS: sweat + alcohol evaporation. NERVE CONDUCTION velocity: up to 120 m/s (fast fibres). SLEEP ~1/3 of life = ~25 years. DIGESTIVE TRACT TOTAL length: mouth to anus ~9 m. AIRWAY length: mouth to alveoli ~30 cm + alveolar surface area 70 m². EYE — focal length adjusts; can distinguish 1-10 million colors + up to 10 million shades; images inverted on retina, brain flips. EAR — audible frequency 20 Hz-20 kHz (young), narrows with age. Dogs 40 Hz-60 kHz (4-fold). TOUCH receptors: Meissner + Merkel + Pacinian + Ruffini corpuscles. PAIN — nociceptors; morphine, endorphins block. TASTE: 5 basic (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) + fat? calcium? debated. SMELL: 400 types of receptors; can distinguish 1 trillion scents.
